ideas.title: Pakistan Is Now Officially a Middle Eastern Economy
ideas.trend: The World Bank moved Pakistan from South Asia to MENAAP effective July 2025, with a Foreign Policy analysis (April 29, 2026) highlighting the institutional consequences now coming into focus.
ideas.consensus: This is a bureaucratic reclassification with minimal real-world impact on Pakistan's economy or development trajectory.
ideas.angle: The reclassification redirects a $40 billion World Bank program, changes Pakistan's development benchmarks from India/Bangladesh to Egypt/Jordan, and hands Pakistani policymakers the Gulf's state-led sovereign capital playbook instead of South Asia's poverty-reduction framework.

content_pack.x_longform:
The World Bank just quietly moved Pakistan out of South Asia and into MENA, and almost nobody is treating it as the structural event it is.

The statistical consequences are immediate. MENAAP's population jumps from 519 million to 813 million. The group's per-capita GDP drops more than 30 percent. Pakistan, with 240 million people, now represents nearly one-third of the entire region's headcount.

But the numbers that matter most are operational. A $40 billion World Bank program, signed last year and running through 2035, now gets managed under the MENAAP vice presidency. Country directors change. Regional trust funds change. Policy benchmarks change. Pakistan no longer gets compared to India and Bangladesh. The comparison set becomes Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco.

That matters enormously.

South Asia's development playbook is built around poverty reduction, agricultural productivity, and incremental integration with global supply chains. The MENA playbook is built around state-led capital deployment, sovereign wealth vehicles, and energy-to-diversification transitions. Pakistan is now being handed the second manual.

The remittance connection already anchors this. More than half of Pakistan's $38.3 billion in FY2025 remittances originated from GCC states. Saudi Arabia sent $739.6 million in January 2026 alone. The UAE sent $694.2 million in the same month. The economic center of gravity has been Middle Eastern for years. The classification just caught up.

My read: Pakistan does not become a Gulf state. But the institutional frameworks that govern how development money flows, which benchmarks are used, and which success stories get replicated now pull from a fundamentally different model.

The chapter called 'South Asia's problem country' is over.

South Asia's playbook: poverty reduction, ag productivity, incremental trade integration. MENA's playbook: state-led capital, sovereign wealth vehicles, energy-to-diversification. Pakistan just got handed the second manual.

The classification 'South Asia's problem country' just ended. What replaces it is not determined yet. But the playbook has changed.
content_pack.substack_draft:
My read: the World Bank reclassifying Pakistan from South Asia to MENA feels, on the surface, like a filing cabinet reorganization. But I've been watching how institutional frameworks shape on-the-ground outcomes long enough to know that vice presidencies matter. When Pakistan moves into MENAAP, the $40 billion World Bank program running through 2035 moves with it. Country directors change. Regional trust funds change. The comparison economies Pakistan gets benchmarked against shift from India and Bangladesh to Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco.

That last part may be the most consequential. South Asia's development playbook centers on poverty reduction and incremental trade integration. The MENA playbook is built around state-led capital deployment, sovereign wealth vehicles, and economic diversification. These are not the same manual. Pakistan's policymakers are now handed the second one.

The remittance flows were already pointing this direction. More than half of Pakistan's $38.3 billion in FY2025 remittances originated from GCC states. The economic center of gravity has been Middle Eastern for years before this reclassification.

Whether this produces better outcomes for ordinary Pakistanis, or just shifts which elites get which phone calls from Washington, is genuinely unclear to me. What is not unclear: the frameworks have changed, and frameworks shape what gets built.

ideas.title: The Seat Model Didn't Die Because AI Is Good. It Died Because Customers Are.
ideas.trend: Software forward P/E multiples hit 22.7x in Q1 2026, trading below the S&P 500 for the first time in history, as AI-driven seat compression produces the first-ever enterprise seat count declines at major vendors including Atlassian.
ideas.consensus: SaaS is being disrupted by AI building competing products that replicate or replace software functionality.
ideas.angle: The disruption isn't AI building a better Jira — it's AI replacing the humans who used Jira. Companies don't need fewer products; they need fewer seats. The collapse is a pricing architecture story, not a product relevance story. Survivors won't be AI-featured incumbents; they'll be whoever invents a business model that doesn't depend on headcount.

content_pack.x_longform:
Software is not being disrupted by competing products. Software is being disrupted by its own customers getting more efficient. That distinction matters.

AI does not replace Jira. It replaces the humans using Jira. Atlassian reported its first-ever enterprise seat count decline in 2026. The tool did not get worse. The workforce using it shrank. The revenue consequence is identical to losing a customer, except the customer never left.

The market has noticed. Software forward P/E multiples averaged 84.1x between May 2020 and May 2022. By Q1 2026, that number is 22.7x, below the S&P 500 multiple for the first time in history. $2 trillion in enterprise software market cap erased in the first wave.

The mechanism is straightforward. If AI agents compress a 500-seat deployment to 100 seats, the vendor's revenue drops 80 percent. The software did not fail. The economics did. Some categories are hitting 30 to 40 percent seat reductions already. Others are at 80 to 90 percent, the threshold where the product becomes economically irrational to keep regardless of quality.

The pricing model was always the vulnerability. Per-seat worked when humans were the unit of production. They no longer are.

Gartner estimates 40 percent of enterprise SaaS spend will include outcome-based elements by 2030, up from 15 percent two years ago. Salesforce moved first with per-conversation Agentforce pricing. AI-native products are operating at 52 percent gross margins, structurally below the 75 to 85 percent legacy SaaS was built on.

My honest takeaway: the question is not whether SaaS survives AI. It is whether the pricing architecture survives. The product is fine. The business model is the problem.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Something about the SaaS collapse in 2026 keeps getting misframed. The popular story is that AI is replacing software products. The accurate story is that AI is replacing the humans using them.

Atlassian's first-ever enterprise seat count decline this year is the clearest example I've seen. Nobody switched away from Jira. The teams using Jira just got smaller, because AI agents absorbed the tasks those seats were paying for. Revenue fell as if they'd lost the customer. The customer never left.

I find this distinction important because it changes what survives. The tools that win aren't necessarily the ones that build the best AI features. They're the ones that invent a pricing model that doesn't depend on headcount. Software forward P/E multiples have fallen from an average of 84.1x in 2020-22 to 22.7x today, below the S&P 500 for the first time in history. The market isn't just pricing in AI risk. It's repricing the business model itself.

The real question I keep returning to: what does an enterprise software company look like when the unit of production is no longer a person? Salesforce's per-conversation Agentforce pricing is the most visible experiment. Whether outcome-based models can sustain the margins that made SaaS the best business in technology history is genuinely unclear to me.

ideas.title: Stablecoins Just Went Mainstream. Nobody Holding Crypto Required.
ideas.trend: Circle launched CPN Managed Payments on April 8, 2026, enabling banks and PSPs to settle via USDC across 20+ blockchains while interacting entirely in fiat. USDC's cumulative onchain settlement has surpassed $70 trillion.
ideas.consensus: Stablecoin adoption is measured by how many consumers and businesses hold digital assets.
ideas.angle: The actual adoption inflection removed the requirement to hold digital assets entirely. Banks and PSPs now get stablecoin-speed settlement with fiat-only interfaces — the stablecoin era as invisible TCP/IP infrastructure, not as wallets.

content_pack.x_longform:
The stablecoin inflection everyone expected to look like mass crypto adoption looks nothing like that.

Circle launched CPN Managed Payments on April 8. Banks and payment service providers now settle in USDC, using 20-plus blockchain rails, without ever holding, minting, or even seeing a digital asset. Circle manages the full lifecycle: minting, burning, compliance controls, blockchain infrastructure. The counterparties interact entirely in fiat.

This is the abstraction layer that makes stablecoin infrastructure real.

USDC has supported $70 trillion in cumulative onchain settlement. Onchain transaction volume hit $12 trillion in Q4 2025 alone. Total stablecoin supply reached $315 billion in Q1 2026, up $8 billion quarter-over-quarter. USDC itself grew 220 percent since late 2023 to $78 billion. These are not speculative numbers. These are settlement infrastructure numbers.

The launch partners are revealing. Thunes and Worldline are not crypto companies. They are payment rails covering emerging markets and European banking respectively. The product is not for crypto-native businesses. It is for the institutions that currently run SWIFT and SEPA and are looking at settlement times and correspondent banking fees and deciding there is a better architecture.

The regulatory piece accelerated this. A UK supplementary compliance regime for stablecoins comes into force May 7, 2026. The infrastructure and the regulation are arriving at the same time.

My read: the stablecoin story is not about wallets and adoption rates among retail users. It is about invisible settlement infrastructure that the average payment recipient will never see, the same way they do not see TCP/IP when an email arrives.

That chapter has already started.

My read: the stablecoin era arrived the same way the internet arrived in banking. Not through a consumer app but through back-end infrastructure that made consumer apps possible.
content_pack.substack_draft:
My take: the dominant stablecoin narrative is about consumers — how many wallets exist, who holds USDC, whether normies are using crypto. I think the actual inflection just happened on the other side of that transaction.

Circle launched CPN Managed Payments earlier this month. Banks and PSPs now access stablecoin-speed settlement without ever holding a digital asset. Circle manages the full stack — minting, burning, compliance, blockchain routing — while the counterparty works entirely in fiat. The stablecoin rails are invisible to the end user and, increasingly, to the institution using them.

USDC has now supported $70 trillion in cumulative onchain settlement. Onchain volume was $12 trillion in Q4 2025 alone. The early partners — Thunes and Worldline — are not crypto-native. Thunes covers emerging market payment corridors. Worldline handles European banking. These are the people running SWIFT and SEPA today.

This is what infrastructure-layer adoption looks like. The same way most people sent email without knowing what TCP/IP was, most people will receive payments settled on stablecoin rails without ever holding a token. Whether the abstraction layer stays with Circle or gets commoditized by the rails themselves is the question I don't have an answer to yet.
